rationale: B wins because it is less likely to get the founder embarrassed by a basic fact-check. Its best framing, "Canva says it has 220M monthly users and 24,000 paying teams — what does that actually convert to in enterprise?", treats the numbers as a question to report. A has more routes, but "Canva has converted just 24,000 of its 220 million users into paying teams" mangles users versus teams and turns an inference into a headline.
gaps_in_A: "Canva has converted just 24,000 of its 220 million users into paying teams" — teams are not users, and the update does not say these are converted free users or Enterprise customers.
"Canva finally builds the SSO and admin controls IT departments were blocking it for" — the SSO/admin angle is real; the claim that IT departments were blocking Canva is not in the facts.
"growth funded by profit" — private and profitable does not prove the enterprise push or acquisition was funded by profit, or that there is a deliberate no-public-markets strategy.
"brand-safe image generation beats generic AI tools" — brand safety, generic-tool comparison, and proprietary capability are not supplied facts; they need reporting before they become the angle.
gaps_in_B: "workflow Adobe Firefly and Microsoft Designer occupy" — those named products are outside the supplied update and need sourcing before they sit inside the pitch.
"Why CIOs should care about Canva's SSO" as a refused angle misses a viable enterprise-procurement story; the feature becomes a story when framed around IT approval and governance.
"Next step: newsjack-detector" is the wrong move for a launch-driven angle set. The next step is proof gathering and a fit-checked journalist list, not hunting for an external peg by default.
"brand-safety/IP questions that follow when AI-generated design enters regulated corporate workflows" reaches past the facts; useful question, but "regulated" and rights-cleared risk need evidence.
